tfn.s: Quiet quitting means an employee has left the job.
tfn.why: The text says: "these people have not actually left their jobs."

tfn.s: Gallup found 20% of employees worldwide were engaged in 2025.
tfn.why: The text says only 20% of employees around the world were engaged in 2025.

tfn.s: Most teams pay workers for overtime.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text says some teams give time off and others pay overtime, but not how many.

tfn.s: Gallup's number does not mean that all the other workers were quiet quitting.
tfn.why: The text says: "This number does not mean that the other 80% were all quiet quitting."

tfn.s: A nurse and an office worker have exactly the same responsibilities.

tfn.s: The same behaviour can be praised in one workplace and criticised in another.
tfn.why: The text says doing contracted hours sounds "unremarkable" where overtime is rare, but may be treated as disloyalty elsewhere.

tfn.s: The writer says healthcare workers deserve unlimited protection, but office staff do not.
tfn.why: The text says: "That does not mean one group deserves unlimited protection and the other unlimited demands."

tfn.s: The writer implies that a worker in a low-paid role may find it harder to set boundaries than a well-paid one.
tfn.why: The text says advice to set boundaries is less useful "when an employee cannot afford to lose their job."

tfn.s: The writer treats Gallup's 20% figure as an estimate of how many employees are quiet quitting.

tfn.s: Praise for going the extra mile can become a problem if it changes what counts as normal effort.

tfn.s: The writer says most workplaces clearly separate contractual duties from voluntary goodwill.

focus.note: Some linkers join two clauses, some need a noun phrase, and some add a result or a contrast across a full stop. Read the whole sentence with your answer in place.

speak.title: Role-play: leaving on time
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: Your employee leaves at five every day and never answers messages in the evening. A big project starts next week. Ask why, and say what you need from the team. You can ask for a small change, or accept the way they work.

b.text: You finish your tasks and leave on time. Your manager wants to talk. Explain why your evenings matter to you. Say what you can offer instead, and what you cannot do.

phrases: I always finish my tasks before I leave.
I'm afraid I'm not available in the evenings.
Can you tell me what you're expecting?
I'd be happy to stay late once a month if it's paid.
That's fair, but we've got a busy week coming.
Could we agree some clear rules?
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class what you agreed. Was it a fair deal for both sides?
